title: Rama spares the spies
hookLine: two spies dressed as monkeys are caught in Rama's camp, and he lets them go unharmed
carry: maryada: dharma keeps its limits in war

cards: The army crosses the bridge and spreads out along Lanka's shore. Across the island, Ravana does what any general would. He sends two of his ministers, Shuka and Sarana, to count the enemy.
They take the shape of monkeys and slip in among the troops. It almost works. But one person in that camp knows exactly what a rakshasa in disguise looks like, because he grew up among them.
Vibhishana sees through them, and they're dragged before Rama.

teach.b: In a war story, you know what usually happens to caught spies, and the monkeys are ready to do it. The two rakshasas, terrified, confess: Ravana sent us to count your army. And Rama laughs.
If you've seen everything, he says, go back.
If you missed anything, look again; Vibhishana will show you around. You're unarmed and you were caught. You won't be killed.
Then he hands them a message for Ravana: show me the strength you relied on when you carried Sita away.
The spies go home, name Rama's leaders one by one from Ravana's tower, and end with advice he doesn't want: make peace and return Sita. Ravana throws them out.
Hindus have a name for Rama that this scene shows: maryada purushottam, the best of men, who keeps the bounds of dharma.
Maryada means a boundary. Rama has every reason to be cruel here: it's war, his wife is a captive, the enemy is spying on him. And still there's a line he won't cross.

Hindu teaching calls this dharma yuddha, righteous war, and the Mahabharata sets out such rules before its own great battle: you don't strike the unarmed, or someone who can't fight back. Rama isn't soft.
His message is a hard one.
But winning doesn't move the line. Today, the spies are more likely to be screenshots.
When you've caught someone in the wrong and could make an example of them, maryada asks one question: is this something a person of dharma does, even when they could?

how: Storytellers often use the release of Shuka and Sarana to show the code of war in the Ramayana: an unarmed messenger or captive is not killed.

o: an army closing in on a city, begun here with spies set free
a sudden raid at night that ends a war in one blow
a truce while both sides gather and count their dead

p: the best of men, who keeps dharma's bounds

s: Rama has the spies put to death
he laughs, lets them look around, and sends them home with a message.
the spies advise Ravana to make peace
after counting the army, they advise returning Sita; Ravana throws them out.
the spies were disguised as monkeys
they took the shape of monkeys to move through the camp.

games.q: you've found an old screenshot that would embarrass someone who hurt you. posting it would win the fight. by Rama's way with the spies, what fits?
o: keep it to yourself: winning doesn't move the line.
post it, but blur the names so it's fair.
games.why: Rama caught the spies red-handed and still sent them home unharmed. maryada: some things a person of dharma doesn't do, even when he could.

practice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp at the family shrine in the evening. Sit before a lamp, or any small light, and fold your hands. Bring to mind someone you're angry with, someone you could hurt if you wanted to.
Breathe slowly, and say to Rama, silently, one line you won't cross with them, however the fight goes. Then bow your head. If you don't pray, simply sit with the light and name the line.

wordCard.voice: The siege. It begins with two spies caught and set free, unharmed, carrying a hard message, because even in war Rama keeps the bounds of dharma.

orig.note: Sanskrit maryādā: a boundary or limit; Rama is called Maryādā Puruṣottama, the best of men, who keeps the bounds of dharma.

carryVoice: Your line: maryada, dharma keeps its limits in war. Next, one last offer at the gates. See you tomorrow.
